extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Department of Education funds (K-12 and postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, institutional legal counsel, policymakers, and other stakeholders implementing Title IX regulations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and responses to public comments on the Department of Education's final Title IX regulations, addressing regulatory justification, scope, institutional obligations, enforcement, and related implementation issues. Intended to inform how recipients should interpret and operationalize specific regulatory provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory justification and evidence standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department may promulgate regulations based on review of case law, enforcement experience, stakeholder feedback, and need — agencies are not required to produce empirical evidence before acting and may adopt prophylactic rules to prevent potential problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Stilwell v. Off. of Thrift Supervision for the proposition that the APA imposes no general obligation to produce empirical evidence; Executive Order 12866 and OMB Circular A-4 direct consideration of qualitative benefits as well as quantitative; the Department relied on available studies, stakeholder input (including public hearings and comments), and enforcement experience. See the Regulatory Impact Analysis for detailed data, costs, and benefits. The Department will not delay regulation merely to compile additional data when qualitative benefits (e.g., psychological wellbeing of students) and existing evidence justify action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for long-lasting, flexible regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Final regulations should be balanced, widely acceptable, and flexible enough to be implemented across a diversity of postsecondary institutions and educational contexts, while providing clarity and settled expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department aims for rules that will endure across administrations by restoring protections, clarifying scope of sex discrimination, and focusing revisions needed to effectuate Title IX. Rules should provide flexibility (e.g., allowing recipients to tailor responses to varied institutions) while ensuring key protections remain (supportive measures, prohibitions against bias/conflicts of interest, ability to consolidate complaints). The Department considered over 240,000 comments in shaping these durable and flexible requirements. Concerns about administrative burden and training are acknowledged and discussed in the Regulatory Impact Analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination with other laws and agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Final regulations apply to Department recipients and should be read in context of other nondiscrimination laws and other agencies' Title IX interpretations, but do not displace other agencies' regulations or create conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department confirms its final regulations apply only to recipients of its Federal financial assistance; recipients that receive funds from multiple agencies are expected to comply with each agency's implementing regulations. The Department has primary responsibility for enforcement regarding its recipients and does not condition other agencies' funding on compliance with these final regs. The Department intends to coordinate with other Federal agencies where appropriate to promote consistent enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family Policymaking Assessment applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment requirements under the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act of 1999 apply to policies and regulations that may affect family well-being; the Department reviewed applicable requirements and determined these final regulations, which apply to recipients, do not directly regulate families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters requested a Family Policymaking Assessment; the Department states it has reviewed and complied with applicable requirements for promulgating regulations. Because the regulations target recipients of Federal financial assistance and not families directly, additional family-specific assessment was unnecessary. See 5 U.S.C. 601 note for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection regardless of national origin or immigration status; retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX protections extend to individuals regardless of national origin, immigration status, or citizenship, and threatening deportation or invoking immigration status to intimidate or deter a Title IX complaint can constitute retaliation if done to interfere with a protected activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department references Supreme Court precedent protecting undocumented students' equal right to public education. Retaliation is defined in §§ 106.2 and 106.71; conduct that threatens deportation with the purpose of interfering with Title IX rights falls within that definition, so no additional regulatory text was deemed necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of employment under Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX applies to any person, including employees, in an education program or activity receiving Department funds; the Department has authority to issue regulations covering employment-related discrimination occurring under an education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department points to 20 U.S.C. 1681 and prior regulatory history to explain that Title IX has not been limited to students. The final regs apply to employees but do not derogate rights under Title VII; recipients may need to comply with both statutes and their implementing regulations. The Department sees no inherent conflict between Title IX and Title VII and declines to remove employment-related provisions (see § 106.57).

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding and 'unfunded mandate' concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX imposes legal obligations on recipients but does not itself provide appropriated funds to implement compliance; the final regulations clarify legal obligations without addressing funding sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department acknowledges costs recipients may incur and that Congress does not appropriate funds through Title IX; recipients must identify funding sources (including congressional appropriations) for compliance. The Regulatory Impact Analysis addresses costs and benefits in detail, but the rule does not create funding mechanisms nor purport to allocate federal funds to cover compliance costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of technical assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department will offer technical assistance to recipients to support implementation of the final regulations, including sample policies, procedures, training materials, and guidance on interactions with other laws (FERPA, Equal Access Act, Title VI, IDEA, Section 504).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR and the Department will provide assistance and contact points (OCR contact page; Equity Assistance Centers; Student Privacy Policy Office). Technical assistance will be tailored, with emphasis on supporting smaller and less-resourced recipients and K-12 institutions. The Department agrees supplemental resources can reduce implementation burden and will provide them as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intra-agency and interagency coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department will coordinate within itself and with other Federal agencies (e.g., DOJ) on programs with similar or overlapping purposes to promote consistent enforcement and efficient implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References Executive Order 12250 directing AG coordination on Title IX, and the Department's commitment to share data and coordinate among Department offices when appropriate. Final regulations still apply only to Department recipients, but coordination is encouraged to harmonize enforcement across related statutory programs (e.g., VAWA 2022, Clery Act).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology: use of 'person' versus 'student/employee'
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations use 'person' to reflect Title IX's coverage of any person in a recipient's education program or activity; use of terms like 'student' or 'employee' in places is to impose specific, targeted obligations, not to narrow protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains that longstanding regulatory terminology choice ensures broad protection while clarifying when particular actions or duties apply to applicants, students, or employees. Definitions such as 'complainant' and hostile environment provisions use 'person' to maintain broad applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline of student organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Student organizations are not respondents under the grievance procedure (cannot be subject to a § 106.45 or § 106.46 proceeding), though recipients must take prompt, effective steps to address sex discrimination that affects organizations and may discipline organizations under their own codes of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department clarifies organizations do not receive due process rights under the grievance procedures, but recipients may act against organizations through other disciplinary authorities; actions directed at organizations are not precluded by these final regulations. Individuals or groups who believe they were discriminated against may file complaints with OCR for investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for contractors and vendors
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may not absolve themselves of Title IX obligations by delegating operations to contractors, subcontractors, or vendors; recipients must provide assurances and ensure third parties do not discriminate in violation of Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites §§ 106.4(a), (c) and the OCR Assurance of Compliance form; recipients must ensure contractors comply and may be responsible for discriminatory conduct by third parties. The Department declines to issue blanket pronouncements about monitoring software applicability since that depends on facts; individuals may file complaints with OCR regarding contractor conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data collection and climate surveys discretion and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are permitted, but not required by these final regulations, to collect and disaggregate demographic data about Title IX complaints and to conduct campus climate surveys; such collection must comply with nondisclosure obligations and other laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department did not propose specific changes to the Civil Rights Data Collection (CRDC) in the NPRM and will solicit comments before altering data collection practices. Recipients may use climate surveys at their discretion to assess barriers to reporting (see § 106.44(b)). VAWA 2022 mandates development of an online survey tool for postsecondary institutions on experiences with violence/harassment; postsecondary recipients must administer that tool and publish campus-level results once developed. K-12 institutions may adapt the tool and consult Department resources (National Center on Safe Supportive Learning Environments) for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: OCR enforcement authority and practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department has statutory authority to enforce Title IX (including suspension or termination of federal funds) and may require remedial actions, equitable relief, injunctive actions, or financial compensation where appropriate; OCR uses voluntary resolution agreements and other enforcement tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References 20 U.S.C. 1682 and 34 CFR 100.8 (incorporated in § 106.81) as bases for remedies including suspension/termination of funds and other lawful means. The Department states voluntary resolution agreements have been effective but may initiate administrative proceedings or refer to DOJ if recipients fail to comply. OCR publishes resolution agreements publicly and will continue to highlight cases. The Department declines to create a 'safe harbor' for recipients who partially comply, emphasizing full compliance is necessary. Case processing times vary by facts; changes to OCR complaint procedures were not proposed in the NPRM and would require additional public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability of regulatory provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Each provision of the final regulations serves an important, related, but distinct purpose and is intended to operate independently, with severability clauses remaining applicable so the invalidity of one provision does not affect others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department cites prior preambles and case law (e.g., Mayor of Baltimore v. Azar) to explain that provisions such as the prohibition on retaliation (§ 106.71), scope of hostile environment (§ 106.11), and grievance procedure requirements (§ 106.45(b)(6)) are meant to function separately. The Department includes explicit references to continued applicability of severability clauses in part 106 (e.g., §§ 106.9, 106.16, 106.24, 106.48, 106.62, 106.72, 106.82).
